answer.label: Misquoted — the real line says ‘many,’ not ‘some’
answer.sourceLine: Hemingway did write this passage — in A Farewell to Arms (1929) — but the actual sentence reads “the world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places,” not “some.” The popular online version swaps that one word and is usually clipped before the darker sentence that follows it in the novel.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “...afterward many are strong at the broken places.”

source.excerpt: If people bring so much courage to this world the world has to kill them to break them, so of course it kills them. The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry.
trail: Frederic Henry's musing appears in Book Four, Chapter XXXIV of A Farewell to Arms (1929), shortly after he and Catherine reunite in Stresa.
Wikiquote's entry for Hemingway lists the passage among the novel's genuine quotes, giving the original wording “many are strong at the broken places” — see Wikiquote ↗.
A 2017 essay tracing the quote's drift documents how “many” became “some” online, and how the line was later spliced with a Leonard Cohen lyric; see whatwouldbaledo.com ↗.
Independent quote-reference transcriptions at Quotepark ↗ and Quotes.net ↗ both give “many,” not “some.”
source.excerptNote: This is Hemingway's actual wording, transcribed from the novel. The version beginning “some are strong” that circulates online is a later paraphrase, not the original text.

author.bio: Hemingway won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature and the 1953 Pulitzer Prize for The Old Man and the Sea. A Farewell to Arms (1929), his semi-autobiographical novel of a wounded American ambulance officer and a British nurse during World War I, remains one of his most widely read books.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The idea and the passage are genuinely Hemingway's, but the wording that circulates online has drifted from what he actually wrote — and it is sometimes spliced with an unrelated quote entirely.

items.why: The widely shared version reads “...afterward some are strong at the broken places,” but Hemingway's actual text says “many are strong at the broken places” — confirmed by Wikiquote ↗ and independently catalogued by a 2017 quote-tracing essay ↗.

A related fabrication, “We are all broken — that's how the light gets in,” blends this Hemingway passage with Leonard Cohen's “Anthem” lyric (“There is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in”) and presents the hybrid as a single Hemingway quote; see whatwouldbaledo.com ↗.

Motivational reposts almost always end at “strong at the broken places,” omitting Hemingway's very next sentence — “But those that will not break it kills” — which turns an uplifting-sounding line into a much grimmer statement about who survives; see the full passage transcribed at Quotes.net ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Hemingway really wrote this passage in A Farewell to Arms (1929) — just with “many,” not “some,” and followed by a much bleaker sentence that inspirational reposts leave out.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Frederic Henry, Hemingway's wounded American narrator, thinks this to himself late in the novel while recovering with Catherine Barkley in Stresa, Italy — not long before their circumstances turn tragic. In its original form the line is less a triumphant motivational slogan than a piece of grim wartime philosophy: most people are broken by the world, some grow stronger at the break, and the ones who refuse to break at all get killed outright.

The single-sentence, inspirational-poster version — “some are strong at the broken places” — has outpaced the real text online, stripped of its bleaker second half and quietly swapped from “many” to “some.”
context.pull: “But those that will not break it kills.”
